{"query":"What are some recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning which can improve effectiveness and adaptability of 5G closed-loop network automation?","report":"Background and Fundamentals

Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, achieving state-of-the-art results in Atari video games, surpassing human performance in board games like Go and chess, and controlling complex systems like magnetic fields in tokamaks (Edvardsen et al., 2022) (Schrittwieser et al., 2019). The integration of DRL into 5G networks has become feasible through the adoption of Radio Intelligent Controller (RIC) platforms, which support near-real-time closed-loop control down to 10 milliseconds and provide a rich action space for RL agents (Edvardsen et al., 2022). This enables RL agents without domain-specific knowledge to learn how to efficiently adjust Radio Access Network (RAN) parameters to match offline optimization in static scenarios while adapting on the fly in dynamic scenarios to improve overall user experience (Edvardsen et al., 2022).

In the context of 5G radio resource allocation, DRL agents learn to make optimal decisions based on rewards and penalties received from the network environment, allocating resources such as frequency bands and power levels to different devices and services to maximize performance metrics like throughput or energy efficiency (G et al., 2023). The approach has shown particular promise in dynamic and unpredictable network conditions, outperforming traditional methods in various scenarios (G et al., 2023). Modern RL frameworks are being developed to coordinate the execution of concurrent analytics tasks across different hardware targets, forming the foundation for intelligent network automation systems (Ruzomberka et al., 2023).
Core RL Algorithm Advancements

Several core RL algorithms have proven valuable for 5G network control problems, including Q-Learning (QL), Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) (Abbas et al., 2023). However, traditional approaches face limitations in scalability and stability when deployed in distributed 5G environments, leading to important algorithmic improvements.

The improved Double Deep Q-Network (IDDQN) addresses long-term stability issues in agent training, showing convergence at least 2 times faster than standard Q-Learning while deviating only 8% from optimal solutions in network slicing applications (Majumdar et al., 2024). This enhanced stability makes IDDQN particularly suitable for managing distributed 6G network deployments where multiple agents must coordinate effectively.

Ensemble-based approaches have emerged as promising solutions to overcome estimation biases in Q-learning. Self-play ensemble Q-learning utilizes multiple Q-tables with various exploration-exploitation rates, enabling agents to choose the most suitable actions while reducing overestimation effects through self-play mechanisms (Salehi et al., 2024). Double Q-learning and ensemble bootstrapped Q-learning methods further mitigate both over-estimation and under-estimation biases by using multiple value functions for action selection and evaluation (Salehi et al., 2024) (Peer et al., 2021) (Wang et al., 2023).

For specific 5G applications, specialized RL frameworks have been developed. Q-learning approaches incorporating hybrid automatic repeat request (HARQ) data and channel state information (CSI) feedback enable seamless transitions between modulation and coding schemes in link adaptation (Huo et al., 2024) (Wu et al., 2020). Deep Q-Network variants combined with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) allow dynamic adjustment of adaptive modulation and coding parameters without relying on predefined block error rate targets (Huo et al., 2024).

Policy gradient-based reinforcement learning has shown effectiveness in computing resource allocation within O-RAN architectures, successfully balancing resources between enhanced Mobile Broadband (eMBB) and Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications (URLLC) users while achieving performance within 6% of optimal integer linear programming solutions (Ejaz et al., 2025) (Sharara et al., 2022). Additionally, Proximal Policy Optimization combined with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks has demonstrated the ability to handle variable latency inherent in 5G networks, with agents successfully adapting their control strategies in response to latency fluctuations (Gilerson et al., 2025).
Robustness and Generalization Improvements

A major limitation of current RL approaches in 5G networks is their tendency to overfit to specific training environments, lacking robustness against unseen conditions and failing to generalize in different environments (Miuccio et al., 2022). This overfitting problem significantly impacts the practical deployment of DRL-based network automation systems, as models typically become highly specialized to their training scenarios and require extensive retraining and fine-tuning for new conditions (Hu et al., 2024).

To address these generalization challenges, observation abstraction techniques have emerged as a promising solution. Instead of learning policies in high-dimensional and redundant observation spaces, these approaches leverage observation abstraction rooted in extracting useful information from the environment, allowing for more robust communication protocols with better generalization capabilities (Miuccio et al., 2022). Autoencoder-based architectures integrated into multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) frameworks demonstrate this approach effectively.

Transfer learning has gained significant attention as a method to improve model reproducibility and sample efficiency in wireless communications (Hu et al., 2024). By leveraging prior knowledge from relevant tasks, transfer learning rapidly adapts pre-solved solutions to new tasks, reducing both processing time and data demand (Wang et al., 2021) (Parera et al., 2020) (Zeng et al., 2020) (Huynh et al., 2022) (Shen et al., 2018) (Pan et al., 2010). These frameworks can tackle task mismatch issues with only a few additional unlabeled training samples, achieving comparable performance to models trained from scratch while requiring much less training time (Shen et al., 2018).

Model-based RL approaches offer another path to improved robustness through novel modeling strategies. Kernel-based RL approaches that combine kernel-based classifiers with self-assessment mechanisms clearly outperform traditional RL algorithms in terms of service level agreement fulfillment, resource efficiency, and computational overhead (Alcaraz et al., 2023). These advances represent important steps toward making RL-based 5G network automation more reliable and adaptable to diverse real-world deployment scenarios.
Multi-Agent and Hierarchical RL Frameworks

The complexity of 5G networks requires coordination across multiple network elements, leading to the development of sophisticated multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) frameworks. Multi-agent systems can optimize mobile network configurations globally using value decomposition approaches that train from a global reward function rather than relying on ad-hoc decomposition of network performance across different cells (Bouton et al., 2023). These algorithms use graph neural network architectures that generalize to different network topologies and learn coordination behaviors effectively.

For critical network operations like network slicing, safe multi-agent architectures have become essential. SafeRL frameworks provide modular, multi-agent approaches for distributed slice orchestration, particularly important for Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication services where RL agent actions can have high or irreversible impact on network services (Dalgkitsis et al., 2022). These frameworks ensure safety during real-time slice orchestration while maintaining improved performance over competing solutions.

Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (MADRL) frameworks that incorporate both centralized and distributed learning with distributed inference increase flexibility and adaptability, empowering individual nodes to manage diverse traffic loads and environmental conditions effectively (Keshtiarast et al., 2024). This approach extends to emerging technologies like 5G New Radio Unlicensed (5G NR-U), demonstrating versatility across different wireless technologies.

Hierarchical RL frameworks decompose complex network problems into bi-level architectures with hierarchical intelligence. The hierarchical deep-Q-learning (h-DQN) framework for traffic steering uses meta-controllers that make long-term and high-level policies, while lower-level controllers execute instant traffic steering actions under these high-level policies (Habib et al., 2024). This approach contrasts with existing single-layer architectures that use standalone agents.

In resource allocation scenarios, hierarchical schemes solve coordination between multiple base stations and users, where multi-agent reinforcement learning determines user priority and scheduled packet numbers, while underlying schedulers handle actual resource allocation (Zhang et al., 2024) (Fan et al., 2020) (Shafieirad et al., 2022). These frameworks have evolved from traditional reactive coordination methods toward proactive and cognitive coordination through data-driven algorithms, including multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches that enhance system ability to detect and mitigate emerging conflicts under dynamic network conditions (Cinemre et al., 2025) (Moysen et al., 2018).
Specific 5G Network Applications

Recent research has demonstrated practical RL deployments across several key 5G network domains:

**Network Slicing and Resource Management:**
- Zero-touch network slice control using DRL to reduce energy consumption, delays, and initialization costs (Ma et al., 2022) (Rezazadeh et al., 2021)
- DynamicSlicerNet for dynamic 5G network slicing tailored to IoT device requirements, achieving 30% latency reduction and 20% reliability improvement (Mahesh et al., 2024)
- Automated slice creation and orchestration using DRL modeled as Markov Decision Problems, with throughput as the primary reward signal (Okello et al., 2024)
- Semantic analysis-integrated network slicing (SA-INS) combining Q-learning with NOMA and network slicing for 15% improvement in prioritization accuracy (Islam et al., 2025)

**Edge Computing and Task Offloading:**
- Container-based cloud native wireless architectures using DRL for Multi-Access Edge Computing optimization (Wang et al._1, 2023)
- TD3-based frameworks for task assignment and load balancing in heterogeneous 5G edge computing environments, specifically targeting Cooperative Intelligent Transportation Systems (Saad et al., 2025)
- Multi-slice resource allocation for URLLC and mMTC using Deep Q-Learning and Proximal Policy Optimization for offloading strategy optimization (Ebrahimi et al., 2025)

**Physical Resource Optimization:**
- Physical Resource Block (PRB) assignment using RL achieving mean performance scores of 0.631 versus 0.609 for expert policies, with significantly reduced performance variability (Groen et al., 2023)
- QoS-driven traffic distribution in 5G backhaul networks using deep reinforcement learning within zero-touch management frameworks (Ma et al., 2022) (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021)

**Advanced QoS Management:**
- OptiAllocRL achieving 40% latency reduction and 25% throughput increase in resource allocation (Mahesh et al., 2024)
- AdaptiveQoSDL minimizing packet loss by 50% and enhancing end-to-end delay by 35% under fluctuating network conditions (Mahesh et al., 2024)
Safety and Real-time Implementation



Real-time implementation challenges center on the computational overhead of neural network inference in production environments. While training RL policies optimized for stringent network requirements is feasible, the adoption of neural network models in real deployments poses significant challenges regarding real-time inference and interpretability (Martins et al., 2024). Deep symbolic regression methodologies address these limitations by converting trained RL policies into closed-form expressions that approximate baseline performance while enabling direct implementation in any programming language (Martins et al., 2024).



For URLLC applications specifically, advanced statistical methods like Thompson Sampling integrated into TD3 algorithms enhance learning capabilities and strategic action selection processes, paving the way for intelligent and autonomous network management solutions that can adapt swiftly to dynamic network conditions (Sohaib et al., 2024). These AI-augmented systems demonstrate superior performance over traditional mechanisms in speed, accuracy, and adaptability while maintaining alignment with zero-touch network management paradigms essential for scalable deployment (Hayatu et al., 2023).
Advanced Learning Paradigms

Continual Learning (CL) has emerged as a promising solution for managing the non-stationary nature of 5G networks, where network configurations and traffic patterns change over time (Lange et al., 2019). Deep Reinforcement Learning combined with continual learning paradigms enables adaptation of learning agents to a series of subsequent tasks that represent different network configurations, allowing agents to quickly converge to efficient resource allocation strategies and adapt to environmental changes without catastrophic forgetting (Lahmer et al., 2023). However, combining CL and DRL for network resource management introduces a significant cost of learning in terms of energy, computation, and communication resources, requiring dynamic strategies to balance resources between the data plane and learning processes while minimizing impact on users' Quality of Service (Lahmer et al., 2023).

Federated learning integration with deep reinforcement learning represents another important paradigm for 5G ultra-dense network environments. This combination enables intelligent multi-time scale resource environment management by using deep reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust resource allocation strategies while employing federated learning to improve model training efficiency and performance while maintaining data privacy (Zhang et al._1, 2024) (Yu et al., 2020). The two-timescale deep reinforcement learning approach integrated with federated learning can reduce task execution time by up to 31.87% in ultra-dense edge computing scenarios (Yu et al., 2020).



Advanced architectural approaches include flexible designs such as multi-agent DRL and incremental learning to support heterogeneous scenarios, along with simulation-driven deployment strategies that use transfer learning to reduce convergence time and service disruptions (Li et al., 2024). These paradigms collectively address the fundamental challenges of deploying RL in dynamic 5G environments while maintaining computational efficiency and adaptation capabilities.
Network Optimization and Performance

Network optimization in 5G systems faces unique challenges related to variable delays and dynamic conditions that require specialized RL formulations. The random-delay-corrected framework addresses scenarios where network delays affect RL performance by modeling the problem as a partial history-dependent MDP (PH-MDP) and transforming it into a standard MDP solvable by traditional DRL algorithms (Du et al., 2022). This approach uses a forward model and delay-corrected trajectory sampling to train agents through continuous interactions, implemented through a delayed-deep-Q-network (delayed-DQN) algorithm that maintains performance despite variable network delays (Du et al., 2022).

For packet-optical network scenarios, RL algorithms can find optimal routing strategies by using measurements from both physical layer (pre-FEC bit error rate and propagation delay) and link layer (link load) information to configure latency-based rewards and penalties (Navarro et al., 2024). These Q-learning based approaches dynamically adapt to changing network conditions by re-calculating optimal policies when link loads change or link degradation occurs, enabling zero-touch networking where the control plane learns from network interactions without human intervention (Navarro et al., 2024).

Hierarchical control architectures offer sophisticated solutions for energy-efficient network management through cooperative deep reinforcement learning methods that include cross-entropy enabled meta-controller policies and cooperative action selections for sub-controllers (Zhou et al., 2023). These architectures enable joint sleep, power, and RIS control across different timescales, increasing flexibility for RAN management and proving particularly important for 6G and O-RAN environments where intelligence spans multiple time scales (Zhou et al., 2023).

Future network optimization strategies are moving toward hybrid systems that combine traditional optimization with machine learning capabilities for more intelligent and adaptable resource management (Yuan et al., 2025). Key advancement areas include adaptive resource allocation using RL for dynamic power optimization, enhanced interference management through ML-based prediction and mitigation, and user-centric optimization that leverages AI to prioritize users based on QoS needs and behavior patterns (Yuan et al., 2025)."}

{"query":"Summarize key research papers that have empirically evaluated open-source 5G testbeds specifically designed for O-RAN?","report":"Background and Context



Several pioneering testbed implementations have demonstrated the feasibility of end-to-end O-RAN research platforms. Notable efforts include the integration of O-RAN compliant software components for closed-loop control in the POWDER testbed, which enables RAN slicing realization through open-source mobility stacks (Upadhyaya et al., 2022) (Johnson et al., 2021). Additionally, advanced automation frameworks like 5G-CT have been developed using Red Hat OpenShift and GitOps paradigms to automatically deploy and test softwarized end-to-end 5G and O-RAN-compliant systems, with real-world validation conducted over-the-air using commercial 5G User Equipment and multiple core networks including Open5GS (Bonati et al., 2023).
Major Open-Source O-RAN Testbed Platforms

**OpenRAN Gym** - The first open, portable toolset for end-to-end design, prototyping, testing, and experimentation of AI/ML O-RAN xApps on heterogeneous wireless experimental platforms (Bonati et al., 2022). OpenRAN Gym provides automated pipelines for data collection, xApp development, and testing workflows for intelligent control in Open RAN systems (Lacava et al., 2023). The framework is platform-independent and has been successfully ported across multiple testbeds including Colosseum, Arena, POWDER, and COSMOS (Bonati et al., 2022) (Raychaudhuri et al., 2020) (Breen et al., 2020).

**ColO-RAN** - The first publicly-available large-scale O-RAN testing framework with software-defined radios-in-the-loop, built on the Colosseum wireless network emulator (Polese et al., 2021) (Bonati et al., 2021). ColO-RAN enables ML research at scale using O-RAN components and programmable base stations, with demonstrated capabilities across 7 base stations and 42 users (Polese et al., 2021).

**OAIC (Open AI Cellular)** - An open-source 3GPP-compliant O-RAN-based 5G testbed developed at Virginia Tech that introduces a Real-Time RIC, zApps, and Z1 interface to support use cases requiring latency less than 10 ms (Upadhyaya et al., 2023). The OAIC testbed includes both control and testing frameworks for AI-based RAN management algorithms (Lacava et al., 2023).

**AERPAW O-RAN Platform** - A scalable open-source O-RAN experimentation platform within the Aerial Experimentation and Research Platform for Advanced Wireless that integrates unmanned aerial vehicles with advanced wireless network technologies (Moore et al., 2024). The platform evaluates FlexRIC as an open-source RAN Intelligent Controller for cellular-connected UAVs.

**Specialized Research Platforms** - Additional platforms include O-RAN-enabled IAB networks integrated into OpenRAN Gym for integrated access and backhaul research (Moro et al., 2023), energy efficiency measurement testbeds combining bare-metal and Kubernetes network functions (Shankaranarayanan et al., 2024), and CF-MIMO O-RAN testbeds capable of serving commercial 5G user equipment (Chu et al., 2025).

**Emerging Integration Frameworks** - Recent developments include open wireless digital twin platforms integrating OpenAirInterface with NVIDIA Sionna RT for high-resolution ray tracing (Iye et al., 2025), enterprise-scale Open RAN testbeds with automated deployment and telemetry collection (Maxenti et al., 2025) (Bahl et al., 2023), and resource-constrained edge device testbeds using Raspberry Pi networks (Hayek et al., 2025).
Empirical Evaluation Methods and Metrics

Empirical evaluation of open-source O-RAN testbeds employs multiple methodologies to assess performance across different network scenarios. **Throughput and latency measurements** represent the most common evaluation metrics, with studies conducting systematic comparisons between different open-source implementations like srsRAN and OpenAirInterface (OAI) (Alam et al., 2024) (Shin, 2024). Researchers evaluate both downlink and uplink performance under controlled conditions, with some studies demonstrating that functional split architectures can enhance flexibility and resource efficiency by offloading processing to distributed units (Alam et al., 2024) (Guemdani et al., 2025).

**Packet-level performance analysis** has emerged as a critical evaluation approach, particularly for multi-user scenarios. Studies conduct over-the-air measurements of packet loss and one-way delay under concurrent uplink and downlink transmissions, showing that open-source O-RAN systems can match or surpass conventional solutions under certain conditions (Alam et al., 2024) (Grohmann et al., 2025). Advanced evaluation methods include security testing through smart jamming attacks that successfully reduce specific user equipment throughput by 100% (Flores et al., 2023).

**Interoperability evaluation** represents another key methodology, where researchers test various open-source RAN and core network combinations to understand integration and performance trade-offs (Alam et al., 2024) (Amini et al., 2024). Studies systematically compare performance across different software combinations, examining factors like UE downlink bit rates, latency, and resource utilization (Amini et al., 2024).

**Specialized evaluation techniques** include positioning accuracy validation using both RF simulator-based setups and real-world O-RAN testbeds (Malik et al., 2024), intelligent surface optimization through extensive measurement experiments in multi-user scenarios (Sahin et al., 2025), and network slice performance evaluation across different spectrum allocation policies (Tsampazi et al., 2025) (Polese et al., 2024). Advanced conflict resolution mechanisms are tested in dedicated O-RAN Open Test and Integration Center environments, demonstrating throughput variability reductions of up to 78% (Sultana et al., 2025).
Key Performance Findings and Results

**Throughput and Latency Performance** - Comparative studies show mixed results across different open-source implementations, with OpenAirInterface 5G RAN winning on downlink rate and latency while srsRAN Project demonstrates superior uplink performance (Amini et al., 2024). However, performance evaluation studies highlight significant limitations, emphasizing that the full potential of 5G remains unrealized primarily due to constraints associated with general-purpose hardware and the current maturity level of open-source software components (Alam et al., 2024) (Hakegard et al., 2024). Despite these limitations, functional split architectures demonstrate enhanced flexibility and resource efficiency by offloading processing to the O-DU (Alam et al., 2024) (Guemdani et al., 2025).

**Multi-User Performance Characteristics** - Packet-level measurements reveal significant variability in performance across multiple concurrent users, with one-way packet delays and packet loss probabilities varying sharply among identical UEs in both closed RAN and open-source O-RAN implementations (Alam et al., 2024) (Grohmann et al., 2025). Notably, studies demonstrate that open-source O-RAN-based systems can, under certain conditions, match or surpass conventional solutions in performance while offering industrial-grade connectivity at lower cost (Alam et al., 2024).

**Dynamic Scaling and Resource Management** - Cloud-native O-RAN testbeds show promising results for dynamic resource management, with systems demonstrating automatic O-DU instantiation when CPU load exceeds 80%, improving throughput and latency under heavy traffic conditions (Alam et al., 2024) (Kim et al., 2024). Advanced deployment strategies achieve cost savings of up to 60% compared to monolithic approaches while maintaining control loop latency requirements (Villa et al., 2024) (Bruno et al., 2024).

**Specialized Application Performance** - Testbed evaluations for specific use cases show promising results, including effective reconfigurable intelligent surface optimization in multi-user scenarios (Sahin et al., 2025), network slice performance improvements across different spectrum allocation policies (Tsampazi et al., 2025) (Polese et al., 2024), and conflict resolution mechanisms that reduce throughput variability by up to 78% (Sultana et al., 2025). Enterprise-scale testbeds demonstrate successful disaggregation of RAN workloads using commodity servers with hardware acceleration, achieving functional separation while maintaining performance requirements (Villa et al., 2024) (Bahl et al., 2023).

**Cross-Platform Compatibility Assessment** - Systematic interoperability evaluation studies test various combinations of open-source RAN and core network software to understand integration challenges and performance trade-offs (Amini et al., 2024) (Alam et al., 2024) (Amini et al._1, 2024). These studies demonstrate that different software combinations yield varying performance characteristics, with OpenAirInterface 5G RAN showing superior downlink performance while srsRAN Project excels in uplink scenarios, though no significant differences emerge between different 5G core implementations (Amini et al._1, 2024).

**Multi-Vendor Integration Frameworks** - Enterprise-scale testbeds demonstrate successful disaggregation of RAN workloads using commodity servers with hardware acceleration, achieving functional separation while maintaining performance requirements (Villa et al., 2024) (Bahl et al., 2023). Advanced automation platforms like NeutRAN provide zero-touch multitenancy through RAN and spectrum sharing, while frameworks such as 5GShell reduce human-based network configurations by automating deployment across different cores and protocol stacks (Maxenti et al., 2025) (Bonati et al._1, 2023) (Mancini et al., 2023).

**Component Configuration Impact** - Research emphasizes that component configurations and interdependencies significantly influence end-to-end performance across different O-RAN implementations (Alam et al., 2024) (Grohmann et al., 2025). Studies show that packet-level performance characteristics can vary sharply among identical user equipment in both closed RAN and open-source O-RAN implementations, with closed-source O-RAN demonstrating more consistent performance patterns across multiple concurrent users (Grohmann et al., 2025).

**Specialized Integration Scenarios** - Integration studies extend to specialized applications including dynamic spectrum sharing with CBRS Base Station Devices integrated with open-source Spectrum Access Systems, ultra-reliable low-latency communication for media applications, and privacy-enhanced data analytics frameworks for hybrid private-public networks (Villa et al., 2024) (Collaco et al., 2023) (Durre et al., 2022) (Zafar et al., 2025). These implementations demonstrate the feasibility of integrating O-RAN components with specialized hardware and software systems while maintaining compliance with open interface specifications."}

{"query":"How do AI/ML-based optimization techniques compare with traditional methods in terms of robustness, generalizability, and efficiency for end-to-end slice management under variable traffic and strict QoS requirements?","report":"Introduction

End-to-end slice management in modern networks requires sophisticated optimization techniques to handle the complex interplay between variable traffic patterns and strict Quality of Service (QoS) requirements. Traditional optimization methods, such as linear programming, heuristic algorithms, and rule-based systems, have long served as the backbone for network resource allocation and management <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. These approaches typically use predefined mathematical models and static parameters to make optimization decisions based on historical data and network assumptions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. In contrast, AI/ML-based optimization techniques leverage machine learning algorithms, including reinforcement learning, deep neural networks, and predictive analytics, to dynamically learn from network behavior and adapt their decision-making processes in real-time <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The fundamental difference lies in how these two paradigms approach uncertainty and change: traditional methods rely on explicit programming and predetermined rules, while AI/ML approaches can discover patterns and relationships in data that may not be immediately obvious to human designers <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This distinction becomes particularly important in slice management scenarios where network conditions can change rapidly and unpredictably, requiring optimization systems that can balance multiple competing objectives such as latency, throughput, and resource utilization across different service types <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.
Robustness Under Variable Traffic and QoS Requirements

Traditional optimization approaches face significant limitations when dealing with variable traffic and strict QoS requirements in network slice management. These methods typically struggle with a lack of timely global information about system states and can yield impractical computations due to excessive model dimensions (Saafi et al., 2022). Traditional traffic management approaches based on queuing theory or static policies prove ineffective due to the dynamic and unpredictable nature of network traffic (Guo et al., 2023). Traditional network models such as queues often fail to capture network complexities accurately, especially in highly dynamic and mobile 5G networks (Sulaiman et al., 2024).

In contrast, AI/ML-based techniques demonstrate superior adaptability and robustness under changing conditions. AI and ML algorithms can learn to map QoS requirements to optimal cross-layer parameters for meeting changing requirements, helping improve network-level throughput, latency, and packet loss while providing improved QoS for large numbers of traffic flows (Zia et al., 2022). Deep reinforcement learning approaches excel at handling complexity and unpredictability, adapting to changing conditions and making decisions based on real-time feedback, while facilitating adaptive resource allocation by adjusting parameters dynamically according to network conditions (Iqbal et al., 2023).

The practical advantages of AI/ML approaches are evident in comparative studies. Deep reinforcement learning-based algorithms for network slice management significantly minimize SLA violations, reducing them to 2.5% for enhanced Mobile Broadband slices and eliminating them entirely for Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications slices compared to traditional algorithms like Round-Robin and Proportional Fair (Navidan et al., 2024). AI optimization strategies leveraging DQN and DDPG algorithms achieve up to 8% increases in throughput, 2ms decreases in latency, and 25% reductions in packet loss compared to conventional methods (Yang et al., 2024). AI/ML systems demonstrate exceptional capacity to outperform conventional algorithms through integrated predictive analytics and dynamic routing capabilities (Tshakwanda et al., 2024).

These improvements stem from AI/ML's ability to enable predictive real-time decision-making and continuous optimization in response to dynamic operating conditions, facilitating intelligent monitoring, prediction, and response to fluctuating network demands (Alam et al., 2024) (Sun et al., 2024). AI-based frameworks provide global optimization capabilities that distinguish them from traditional local optimization methods, enabling rapid decision-making while maintaining interconnected module operations (Pan et al., 2024).
Generalizability Across Network Conditions

Traditional optimization methods face significant generalizability challenges when applied across different network conditions and service types. Conventional optimization algorithms suffer from exponentially growing complexity with network scale, making them unsuitable for large-scale real-time applications (Qin et al., 2024). Traditional network models such as queues often fail to capture network complexities accurately, especially in highly dynamic and mobile 5G networks, while simulation-based methods using packet-level simulators are computationally expensive and may not accurately represent real-world scenarios (Sulaiman et al., 2024). Simple regression-based models adopted by existing approaches fail to capture the complexities of end-to-end networks and may yield sub-optimal results when network conditions deviate from the training environment, demonstrating limited generalizability across diverse network settings (Sulaiman et al., 2024) (Sulaiman et al., 2023).

In contrast, AI/ML-based approaches exhibit remarkable generalizability capabilities across varying network conditions. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) possess strong generalization capabilities that can be exploited to extend ML-based optimization over varying ranges of network topologies, while also capturing inter-layer parameter dependencies and adapting to changing network dynamics, traffic loads, channel conditions, and QoS requirements (Zia et al., 2022) (Zhu et al., 2020). Advanced AI/ML techniques such as Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), GNNs, and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) possess great potential to handle complex cross-layer optimization and study cross-layer interactions that remained bottlenecks in traditional approaches (Zia et al., 2022).

Recent developments in AI-driven methodologies show improved model generalization in dynamic mobile networks. Modern AI optimization strategies demonstrate robustness and scalability across diverse network scales, traffic patterns, and congestion levels, confirming their adaptability and effectiveness in a wide array of operational contexts (Yang et al., 2024). However, learning-based paradigms still face challenges with suboptimal generalization to novel network conditions or previously unseen service demands, requiring extensive task-specific agent engineering and computationally intensive training regimens (Nouri et al., 2024). Despite these challenges, AI/ML systems demonstrate exceptional capacity to outperform conventional algorithms through integrated predictive analytics and dynamic routing capabilities that enhance generalization across different network scenarios (Tshakwanda et al., 2024).
Efficiency and Computational Performance

Traditional optimization methods face significant computational challenges that limit their practical application in dynamic network slice management scenarios. Conventional optimization algorithms suffer from exponentially growing complexity with network scale, making them unsuitable for large-scale real-time applications . Network slicing problems are often modeled as Mixed-integer Linear Programming (MILP) or Nonlinear Integer Programming (NLP) optimization problems, but these are NP-Hard, meaning solutions cannot be efficiently computed for large-scale instances within polynomial time (Ochonu et al., 2024) (Phyu et al., 2023). Traditional optimization methods often lack the agility to cope with rapidly evolving network states and diverse performance criteria, while traditional network models such as queues often fail to capture network complexities accurately, especially in highly dynamic and mobile 5G networks (Iqbal et al., 2023) (Sulaiman et al., 2024). Simulation-based methods using packet-level simulators are computationally expensive and may not accurately represent real-world scenarios, with conventional network simulators being time-intensive and limiting their application for online resource allocation (Sulaiman et al., 2024) (Liu et al., 2021) (Liu et al., 2022) (Ferriol-Galmes et al., 2022).

In contrast, AI/ML-based approaches offer significant computational advantages and scalability benefits. An online AI-based resource allocation decision process has the potential to achieve low complexity after an offline training procedure, which addresses the high computational complexity challenge in conventional model-based optimization methods (Shen et al., 2020) (Sciancalepore et al., 2019). Recent work demonstrates that AI-based solutions are not only faster, but can also scale efficiently compared to traditional heuristic and classical optimization techniques (Tuli et al., 2022) (Wilder et al., 2018) (Tuli et al., 2021) (Tuli et al._1, 2021). ML-based optimization methods can handle real-time problems and achieve their objectives using simpler optimization models, thereby reducing computing power and energy consumption (Liang et al., 2024).

The practical computational benefits of AI/ML approaches are demonstrated through comparative studies showing superior performance metrics. Kernel-based reinforcement learning clearly outperforms traditional RL algorithms in terms of computational overhead, with the importance of low computing times allowing more frequent updates of resource allocation and improved system elasticity (Alcaraz et al., 2023) (Su et al., 2019). However, reinforcement learning does present obstacles due to its high computational complexity, requiring substantial resources and potentially impacting real-time decision-making (Iqbal et al., 2023). Despite these challenges, modern AI methodologies show superior efficiency and effectiveness across various scenarios, with integrated approaches offering improved precision and model generalization while addressing the computational limitations of traditional methods (Nouri et al., 2024) (Feng et al., 2020) (Adhikari et al., 2024).
Practical Implementation Considerations

The practical implementation of AI/ML-based optimization techniques in network slice management demonstrates clear advantages over traditional approaches in several key areas. AI-assisted approaches can cope with the coupling between slice configuration management and infrastructure management to balance the adaptivity and overhead of slicing-based resource management, with simulation results under different data traffic distributions showing that AI-powered slicing-based resource management frameworks outperform benchmark frameworks and achieve close-to-optimal performance in energy efficiency (Zhou et al., 2023).

A major practical advantage of ML-based implementations is their ability to learn and adapt from real network data. ML algorithms can adaptively learn from network data to optimize routing decisions, leading to improved network performance, reduced latency, and enhanced QoS (Serag et al., 2024) (Amin et al., 2021) (Abdalzaher et al., 2022). This learning capability extends to predictive resource management, where ML models can analyze historical traffic patterns and resource usage data to predict future demand and dynamically adjust resource allocations accordingly (Serag et al., 2024) (Schneider et al., 2020).

Modern AI implementations also address the complexity of real-world network slice management through sophisticated optimization approaches. The use of evolutionary algorithms for dynamic resource allocation represents a groundbreaking departure from traditional static allocation methods, allowing networks to continuously adapt to changing conditions while optimizing resource usage and ensuring QoS guarantees in real-time (K et al., 2024). Furthermore, the integration of AI-powered data analytics for data-driven decision-making enables network slicing decisions to be based on real-time insights derived from network traffic, user behavior, and application requirements, thereby allowing for proactive and efficient resource allocation (K et al., 2024).

The application of multi-objective optimization techniques in AI-based implementations acknowledges the complex trade-offs inherent in network slicing and provides a more holistic approach to balancing conflicting objectives (K et al., 2024). This practical consideration is crucial for real-world deployments where multiple performance metrics must be simultaneously optimized while maintaining service quality across different slice types."}

{"query":"Survey recent papers on the use of LLMs for 5G network orchestration","report":"Introduction and Background

The integration of Large Language Models into 5G network orchestration represents an emerging field that aims to revolutionize how networks are managed and controlled. Traditional 5G network orchestration relies on complex, rule-based systems that require specialized expertise to configure and maintain <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Recent research has begun exploring how LLMs can serve as intelligent intermediaries that understand natural language instructions and translate them into specific network management actions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. This approach promises to make network orchestration more accessible to human operators while potentially improving the speed and accuracy of network management decisions <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The core idea is that LLMs can process vast amounts of network data, understand context and intent, and generate appropriate orchestration commands or policies without requiring operators to have deep technical knowledge of underlying network protocols and configurations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Current research focuses on several key areas including intent-based networking, automated service provisioning, network slicing management, and cross-domain orchestration scenarios where LLMs can provide the semantic understanding needed to coordinate complex network operations <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.
Intent-Based Networking and Management

Intent-based networking represents one of the most promising applications of LLMs in 5G network orchestration, where the goal is to reduce human intervention by automatically interpreting and executing network management tasks expressed in natural language (Manias et al., 2024). Recent research has demonstrated that LLMs can effectively bridge the gap between high-level operator intentions and low-level network configurations through sophisticated intent extraction and translation frameworks (Manias et al._1, 2024). 

Several approaches have emerged for implementing LLM-based intent systems. Custom telecom-specific models like TelecomGPT have been fine-tuned for network-specific tasks, while intent translation systems allow users to express requirements in natural language and convert them into Network Service Descriptors (Kherroubi et al., 2024). More advanced implementations use semantic routing to enhance the performance of LLM-assisted intent-based management, showing improved accuracy and efficiency compared to standalone LLM architectures with basic prompting (Manias et al._1, 2024).

The practical applications extend beyond core 5G networks to integrated optical transport infrastructures, where GenAI models translate high-level operator intents into optimization code and create auto-configuration policies for optical networks (Tzanakaki et al., 2024). Early implementations have also integrated chatbot frameworks like RASA for intent translation, though these approaches still require human-in-the-loop validation which limits scalability (Dinh et al., 2025) (Cesila et al., 2023). Other work has focused on NLP interfaces for intent engines that facilitate human-network system interaction for tasks like slice provisioning and service deployment, though direct API mapping remains a challenge (Dinh et al., 2025) (McNamara et al., 2023).
Network Slicing and Service Orchestration

Network slicing represents a critical area where LLMs can transform 5G orchestration by automating the complex process of creating, managing, and optimizing virtualized network segments. Recent research proposes comprehensive frameworks that integrate LLMs with existing Management and Orchestration (MANO) systems to handle the complete slice lifecycle (Dandoush et al., 2024). These frameworks use LLMs to translate user intent into technical requirements, map network functions to infrastructure resources, and manage ongoing slice operations including monitoring, autoscaling, and allocation optimization (Dandoush et al., 2024).

The multi-stakeholder nature of network slicing has led to the development of collaborative LLM frameworks where multiple agents represent different network service providers and negotiate shared resources. The Maestro framework demonstrates this approach by using LLM-based agents that can resolve conflicts and achieve consensus across business, service, and network planes while maintaining comparable accuracy to traditional optimization algorithms (Tang et al., 2025) (Chatzistefanidis et al., 2024). This collaborative approach is particularly valuable for cross-domain slicing scenarios where different administrative domains need to coordinate resource allocation and service delivery.

However, implementing LLMs for end-to-end network slicing faces several challenges including limited dataset availability, computational power requirements, potential security vulnerabilities, and issues with trust, validation, interoperability, and privacy (Dandoush et al., 2024). These limitations highlight the need for continued research into robust and secure LLM integration methods for production network environments.
Multi-Agent and Cross-Domain Orchestration

The complexity of modern network environments has driven research toward multi-agent LLM systems that can orchestrate operations across diverse network domains and technologies. Cross-domain network orchestration using LLMs addresses the challenge of coordinating between different network types, such as robotic domains and optical transport networks, through collaborative multi-agent workflows (Xu et al., 2024). These systems use multiple interacting LLM-powered agents that exchange information and work together to solve problems that exceed the capabilities of individual agents, including real-time topology retrieval, network optimization using physical models, and even physical fiber switching operations (Xu et al., 2024).

Recent developments have introduced reflexive architectures for LLM-powered agents that can autonomously perceive network and application data while acting upon Software-Defined Network environments. These agents go beyond traditional natural language processing tasks by actually interpreting and executing network management actions without human intervention, demonstrating precise control over simulated 5G Core Networks and application-aware optimizations (Araujo et al., 2024).

Specialized multi-agent frameworks have also emerged for simulation and testing scenarios, where different agents handle distinct aspects of network orchestration. These systems coordinate specialized agents for generating simulation scripts, designing tests, executing simulations, and interpreting results using advanced coordination mechanisms, transforming natural language inputs into fully validated network simulation scenarios (Rezazadeh et al., 2025). This division of labor among specialized agents allows for more sophisticated orchestration capabilities that can handle the full lifecycle of network operations from planning through execution and analysis.
Semantic Communication and Routing

Semantic communication represents a paradigm shift in 5G network optimization, where LLMs enable networks to transmit meaning rather than raw bits, leading to more efficient bandwidth utilization. Recent research has demonstrated that semantic routing can significantly enhance the performance of LLM-assisted intent-based management and orchestration of 5G core networks, with results showing improved accuracy and efficiency compared to standalone LLM architectures (Manias et al._1, 2024).




Simulation and Testing Frameworks

The development of LLM-powered simulation and testing frameworks represents a significant advancement in 5G network development and validation processes. Recent research has introduced sophisticated multi-agent frameworks that integrate LLMs with established network simulators like ns-3 to automate the creation, validation, execution, and analysis of 5G/6G simulation scenarios (Rezazadeh et al., 2025). These systems divide the complex simulation process into specialized agents that handle distinct aspects of the workflow, including generating simulation scripts, designing tests, executing simulations, and interpreting results using advanced coordination mechanisms.

The technical implementation of these frameworks leverages structured chain-of-thought reasoning processes combined with retrieval-augmented generation to translate natural language simulation specifications into precise network simulator scripts (Rezazadeh et al., 2025). This approach transforms the traditionally complex process of network simulation setup into a more accessible workflow where operators can specify requirements in natural language and receive fully validated simulation environments.

Beyond simulation frameworks, LLMs are being explored for broader network configuration automation in virtualized and Open RAN environments. Research efforts focus on automatically producing network configurations using language models, with particular attention to mobile radio network and 5G deployments where LLMs generate domain knowledge, code, and network configuration specifications (Maxenti et al., 2025). These developments contribute to the broader goal of simplifying and streamlining network configuration and management processes across the entire 5G ecosystem.
Specific Applications and Use Cases

Recent research has identified several concrete applications where LLMs can enhance 5G network orchestration:

• **Wireless Access Point Optimization**: LLM-based combinatorial optimizers have been developed for wireless network planning tasks, specifically focusing on optimizing the number and placement of wireless access points, showing superior performance compared to traditional algorithms like Ant Colony Optimization, particularly as problem complexity increases (Qiu et al., 2024) (Shokrnezhad et al., 2025)

• **UAV Network Management**: LLMs are being used for trajectory planning and wireless resource allocation in scenarios serving Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, with frameworks that integrate LLMs and graphs for dynamic networking optimization to improve UAV communication and positioning (Sun et al., 2024) (Shokrnezhad et al., 2025)

• **Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS)**: LLM-enhanced RIS systems have been developed for 6G Internet of Vehicles applications, where LLMs analyze channel status, vehicle movement patterns, and quality of service requirements to optimize wireless resource allocation and signal decoding in dynamically changing vehicular environments (Liu et al., 2025) (Shokrnezhad et al., 2025)

• **Integrated Terrestrial-Non-Terrestrial Networks**: LLMs are being explored for intelligent control operations in 6G integrated terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks with IoT services, addressing challenges in resource management, interference cancellation, and handover management across diverse network types (Rong et al., 2024) (Senevirathna et al., 2022)

• **Security and Zero-Touch Operations**: LLMs enable enhanced security features including Intent-Based Networking, Network Data Analytics Function (NWDAF), and zero-touch network security operations, aiming to establish higher standards for safe and intelligent network management (Senevirathna et al., 2022)

• **Multi-Domain Resource Allocation**: Applications extend to multi-domain scenarios addressing both network-cloud integration and terrestrial-non-terrestrial infrastructure coordination, demonstrating LLMs' capability to handle complex cross-domain orchestration requirements (Shokrnezhad et al., 2025)
Challenges and Limitations

Despite the promising developments in LLM-powered 5G network orchestration, several critical challenges limit their practical deployment and effectiveness:

• **Dataset Availability**: Training effective LLMs for network orchestration requires large, high-quality datasets of network operations and configurations, which are often proprietary, limited, or difficult to obtain from network operators (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Computational Power Requirements**: LLMs demand significant computational resources for both training and inference, creating scalability concerns for real-time network orchestration where decisions must be made within strict latency constraints (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Security Vulnerabilities**: Integration of LLMs introduces potential network security backdoors and new attack vectors that could compromise network integrity and create vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Trust and Validation Issues**: The "black box" nature of LLMs makes it difficult to validate their decision-making processes and ensure reliability in mission-critical network operations where failures could have severe consequences (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Interoperability Challenges**: Integrating LLMs with existing network management systems, protocols, and standards requires significant adaptation and may face compatibility issues with legacy infrastructure (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Privacy Concerns**: Network data contains sensitive information about users, traffic patterns, and infrastructure that must be protected when processed by LLMs, especially when using cloud-based or third-party models (Dandoush et al., 2024)

• **Real-time Performance**: Network orchestration often requires sub-second response times, but LLM inference can introduce latency that may not meet the strict timing requirements of 5G networks <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">

{"query":"What approaches can be utilized to model the end-to-end response time of a virtual network function, accounting for processing latency and queuing delays under dynamic traffic conditions?","report":"Background

Virtual Network Functions represent a fundamental shift from dedicated hardware network appliances to software-based implementations running on commodity servers or cloud infrastructure <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Unlike traditional network functions with predictable hardware-based processing times, VNFs introduce additional complexity layers including hypervisor overhead, shared resource contention, and variable processing delays that depend on the underlying virtualization platform <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The end-to-end response time of a VNF encompasses multiple components: packet arrival and queuing at input interfaces, processing time within the VNF software logic, internal queuing between processing stages, and output queuing before packet departure <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. Dynamic traffic conditions further complicate this modeling challenge, as VNFs must handle varying traffic loads, burst patterns, and service demands that can change rapidly over time, leading to non-steady-state behavior that traditional static models cannot adequately capture <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">. The challenge becomes even more complex in service function chaining scenarios where multiple VNFs are connected in sequence, creating interdependent performance relationships where delays in one function can cascade through the entire chain <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-sonnet-4-20250514">.
Queueing Theory Approaches

Classical queueing network models form the backbone of VNF performance analysis, with researchers employing established frameworks like Jackson networks and Baskett-Chandy-Muntz-Palacios (BCMP) networks to analyze average end-to-end delay performance given virtual network topology, traffic arrival rates, and component capacities (Zhang et al., 2017). For more realistic modeling of VNFs with multiple components and service chains, open queueing networks of G/G/m queues provide greater flexibility, offering closed-form expressions to estimate mean response time with a reduced set of input parameters (Prados-Garzon et al., 2017) (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021) (Prados-Garzon et al._1, 2017). These G/G/m models are particularly valuable because they can accommodate general arrival and service distributions while supporting multiple servers, making them suitable for virtualized environments where processing follows space-shared resource allocation policies (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021) (Buyya et al., 2009).

Advanced queueing approaches address the complexity of virtualized infrastructure by modeling the multi-layered delays inherent in VNF processing. Each packet traverses multiple queuing stages: entering the physical node's hypervisor queue, being processed by the hypervisor, entering the virtual machine queue, and receiving service from the VNF instance (Yaghoubpour et al., 2021). This hierarchical queuing structure is often modeled using M/M/1 systems where hypervisor and VNF processing rates can be characterized separately (Yaghoubpour et al., 2021) (Kirchner et al., 2023). More sophisticated models incorporate traffic characteristics like Poisson arrival distributions and varying packet sizes within M/M/1 frameworks to handle non-uniform traffic flows and limited processing capacity constraints (Zhang et al., 2022) (Sun et al., 2019).

Stochastic Network Calculus (SNC) provides an alternative queueing-theoretic approach that can handle both bursty and non-bursty traffic patterns, offering upper and lower delay bounds for VNF chains while addressing resource competition through convolution associativity and leftover service technologies (Fountoulakis et al., 2019) (Miao et al., 2019). For complex service scenarios involving VNF sharing and priority management, researchers employ M/M/1 systems with priority queueing to model how multiple services can share VNF instances while maintaining performance guarantees (Zhang et al., 2022) (Malandrino et al., 2019). Dynamic system stability is addressed through Lyapunov optimization theory applied to queueing models, enabling algorithms that guarantee system stability while fulfilling service requirements (Fountoulakis et al., 2019) (Gu et al., 2019) (Feng et al., 2016).

Specialized queueing methodologies have emerged for specific VNF architectures and use cases. Queuing Petri Nets (QPNs) enable formal specification of VNF behavior including queuing, synchronization, and stochastically distributed processing delays, allowing analysis of complex network services with bidirectional flows and loops (Arteaga et al., 2020) (Schneider et al., 2018). For modern 5G networks, non-product-form queueing networks with G/G/m nodes provide realistic modeling capabilities, using decomposition methods and Allen-Cunneen approximations to analyze interconnected network components (Simone et al., 2024). Tandem queuing models address resource distribution in NFV nodes using approaches like Dominant of Generalized Resource Processing (DR-GPS) to achieve equitable resource utilization across multiple traffic streams (Elagin et al., 2022).
Analytical and Mathematical Programming Models

Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulations represent the dominant mathematical programming approaches for modeling VNF response times within optimization frameworks. These models typically formulate VNF placement and chaining problems with the primary objective of minimizing end-to-end latency while considering processing delays, queuing delays, and propagation delays as constraint functions (Chen et al., 2022) (Xuan et al., 2021). The latency components are often modeled as upper bounds that depend on traffic utilization, with processing and queuing delays tied to node and virtual machine utilization levels, while propagation delays are proportional to physical path lengths (Baumgartner et al., 2015).

Advanced MILP formulations incorporate queueing theory directly into the optimization constraints by modeling VMs as M/M/1 processor-sharing queues, enabling joint optimization of VNF placement and resource allocation while minimizing average service delay (Golkarifard et al., 2021) (Agarwal et al., 2018). These integrated approaches allow the mathematical models to capture both the discrete placement decisions and the continuous performance characteristics of VNF processing under varying load conditions.

Specialized mathematical programming techniques have emerged for specific VNF deployment scenarios and performance objectives. Non-linear integer programming models address complex VNF chaining scenarios where delay relationships are non-linear, often requiring linearization techniques to make problems tractable (Yuan et al., 2020) (Gouareb et al., 2018). Binary Integer Programming (BIP) formulations focus specifically on VNF selection and chaining decisions with end-to-end delay minimization objectives (Asgari et al., 2021) (Pei et al., 2020). Integer Nonlinear Programming (INLP) models provide frameworks for handling both totally ordered and partially ordered service function chains while quantitatively modeling traversing delays (Xuan et al., 2021) (Yang et al., 2019).


Machine Learning and Prediction-Based Approaches

Statistical learning methods offer a fundamental departure from traditional queueing theory by eliminating unrealistic assumptions about network topology and service distributions. Deep mixture density networks (MDNs) can predict the end-to-end delay distribution of service function chains given the network's state, providing a sufficiently general approach that applies across different contexts and applications without requiring specific distributional assumptions (Raeis et al., 2020). This approach models VNFs using queueing theory as a framework while replacing theoretical analysis with statistical learning methods to predict conditional distributions of waiting times in queueing systems, enabling extraction of descriptive statistics like mean, variance, and percentiles for delay announcements and SLA conformance (Raeis et al._1, 2020) (Raeis et al., 2019).

Ensemble learning techniques provide practical solutions for VNF latency prediction by combining multiple predictive models. Random forest algorithms can predict both processing time and queuing time of VNFs to optimize end-to-end delay, offering a stochastic prediction model that handles the variability inherent in VNF processing (Sun et al., 2020). These ensemble approaches are particularly valuable because they can capture complex non-linear relationships between system state variables and performance metrics without requiring explicit mathematical formulations.



Profiling-based prediction frameworks combine data collection with learning algorithms to model VNF performance on given network infrastructure. These solutions collect system resources and workload data to make advance predictions about VNF performance, with specialized frameworks developed for both individual VNFs and network function chains consisting of multiple VNFs connected in series (Rathore et al., 2022) (Asgari et al., 2021) (Yue et al., 2021). This profiling approach enables proactive resource management and placement decisions based on predicted performance characteristics rather than reactive adjustments after performance degradation occurs.
Performance Analysis Tools and Methodologies

The following tools and methodologies provide computational frameworks for analyzing VNF end-to-end response times:

• **Queueing Networks Analyzer (QNA)** - An approximate method for deriving performance metrics of G/G/m queue networks using second-order moments of arrival and service processes, validated experimentally for virtualized network functions like vMME in data center environments (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021)

• **Jackson Networks Analysis** - Classical queueing network methodology used alongside QNA to solve open queueing networks and estimate end-to-end mean response time for service network systems (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021)

• **Mean Value Analysis (MVA)** - Computational technique employed in conjunction with other queueing methodologies to analyze network performance metrics in virtualized environments (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021)

• **Queuing Petri Nets (QPNs)** - Formal specification method that allows expression of queuing, synchronization, stochastically distributed processing delays, and changing traffic characteristics at each VNF, enabling analysis of end-to-end delay, throughput, and queue lengths with support for bidirectional network services containing loops (Arteaga et al., 2020) (Schneider et al., 2018)

• **Decomposition Method with Allen-Cunneen Approximation** - A flexible approach for approximate performance analysis that breaks queueing networks into subsystems, using iterative procedures to calculate squared coefficients of variation of inter-arrival times and employing Allen-Cunneen formulas to derive mean sojourn times (Simone et al., 2024)

• **CloudSim Simulation Toolkit** - Extensible simulation framework that enables modeling and simulation of cloud computing environments, supporting creation of virtual machines, job mapping, and analysis of data center federation policies (Prados-Garzon et al., 2021) (Buyya et al., 2009)

• **Tempus Latency Analysis Framework** - A general method that uses empirical latency measurements to map distributions to queueing, propagation, and transmission delays, applying numerical convolution to obtain overall latency distributions and compute probability of time-bounded reachability between network nodes (Abdous et al., 2024) (Rover et al., 2016)

• **Automated QPN Analysis Tools** - Tool-based workflows that support specification of network services and automatic generation of simulation code for in-depth behavioral and performance analysis, enabling developers to anticipate the impact of different service configurations (Arteaga et al., 2020) (Schneider et al., 2018)
Dynamic and Real-time Modeling Considerations

Dynamic VNF modeling addresses the fundamental challenge of handling traffic uncertainty and non-steady-state behavior that occurs in real network environments. Traffic arrival rates are not always deterministic in practical applications, requiring models that can accommodate varying loads and burst patterns (He et al., 2021). Stochastic models have been developed to handle both processing and transmission flows in systems with service function chaining requirements, providing analytical expressions for end-to-end delay, system throughput, and task drop rates under dynamic conditions (Fountoulakis et al., 2019) (Fountoulakis et al., 2018).



Advanced dynamic modeling techniques incorporate both bursty and non-bursty traffic patterns using Stochastic Network Calculus (SNC) to provide upper and lower delay bounds for VNF chains. These models address resource competition through convolution associativity and leftover service technologies, enabling quantitative investigation of end-to-end performance bounds in NFV networks with dynamic and on-demand features (Miao et al., 2019).

{"query":"Why is the Proof-of-Work (PoW) consensus algorithm unsuitable for energy-constrained blockchain systems, and what characteristics should an alternative consensus mechanism have to achieve energy efficiency without compromising security and scalability?","report":"Introduction: Understanding Proof-of-Work

Proof-of-Work (PoW) serves as the foundational consensus mechanism for blockchain networks, originally introduced by Bitcoin and still widely deployed today (Lathamani et al., 2024) (Yonezawa, 2025). In this system, network participants called miners compete against each other to solve computationally expensive mathematical challenges within a predefined timeframe, such as the 10-minute block time used in Bitcoin (Haddouti et al., 2022). The first miner to find a valid solution earns the right to add a new block to the blockchain and receives associated rewards (Yonezawa, 2025).

PoW ensures network security by making attacks computationally expensive and effectively prevents double-spending (Lathamani et al., 2024) (Yonezawa, 2025). However, this security comes at significant cost through two major issues. First, the mining process requires enormous computational power, leading to excessive energy consumption that rivals entire countries like Poland or Malaysia for Bitcoin alone (Yonezawa, 2025). Second, the reliance on specialized mining hardware (ASICs) creates centralization risks by favoring large-scale operations, leading to concentration of mining power among few entities (Yonezawa, 2025).

These environmental and centralization concerns have prompted researchers to explore alternative consensus mechanisms, including Proof of Stake (PoS) and Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS), which aim to reduce energy consumption while maintaining security (Haddouti et al., 2022) (Saleh, 2020) (Yonezawa, 2025). Unlike PoW's computational competition, PoS selects validators based on their economic stake in the network, requiring participants to prove ownership of blocked cryptocurrency rather than solving energy-intensive puzzles (Haddouti et al., 2022) (Lathamani et al., 2024).
Energy and Resource Limitations of PoW in Constrained Systems

The limitations of PoW become particularly pronounced when deployed in resource-constrained environments such as IoT networks and mobile devices. PoW consensus mechanisms consume enormous amounts of energy, with Bitcoin alone requiring approximately 39-147 TWh annually - equivalent to the electricity consumption of entire countries like Austria, Thailand, or Denmark (Seyitoglu et al., 2021) (Wang, 2023) [273655046 | Fernández-Blanco et al. | 2024 | Citations: 0]. This massive energy consumption stems from the computational wastefulness of traditional PoW algorithms, where miners perform intensive hashing operations to solve cryptographic puzzles that serve no practical purpose beyond securing the blockchain (An et al., 2023) (Males et al., 2023).

For constrained devices, PoW presents multiple insurmountable barriers. The computational requirements are simply too heavy for devices with limited processing power, as the mining difficulty increases exponentially and demands specialized hardware like ASICs (Ngubo et al., 2020) (Caceres et al., 2023) (Nair et al., 2021). IoT devices face particular challenges executing computationally intensive consensus tasks, as their limited resources cannot handle the high computational power required for block mining (Meisami et al., 2023) (Venkatesan et al., 2024). Additionally, PoW implementations like Ethereum's Ethash are too memory-intensive for constrained devices, further limiting their participation in blockchain networks (Ngubo et al., 2020).

The performance limitations of PoW compound these resource constraints. PoW-based systems suffer from low transaction throughput (only 7 transactions per second in Bitcoin), high latency (up to 10 minutes for transaction confirmation), and poor scalability as network size increases (Mavroudis et al., 2020) (Bano et al., 2017) (An et al., 2023) (Venkatesan et al., 2024). These characteristics make PoW unsuitable for real-time IoT applications that require fast response times and high transaction volumes (Deepak et al., 2024) (Ragul et al., 2025).

Most critically, the "high-security" nature of PoW paradoxically reduces overall network security in constrained environments because resource-limited devices cannot meaningfully contribute to the consensus process, regardless of their numbers on the network (Ngubo et al., 2020). This creates a fundamental contradiction where the very devices that could benefit most from blockchain technology are excluded from participating in its security model, limiting the technology's applicability in emerging domains like smart cities and industrial IoT (Abbasi et al., 2024).
Alternative Consensus Mechanisms














Key Characteristics for Energy-Efficient Consensus Mechanisms

Based on the analysis of PoW limitations and existing alternatives, several key characteristics emerge as essential for designing energy-efficient consensus mechanisms suitable for constrained environments. The primary goal is energy efficiency, as any sustainable blockchain system must significantly reduce the computational and energy requirements compared to PoW (Zhao et al., 2020). This efficiency should be achieved without energy-intensive mathematical puzzles or computational competitions that serve no practical purpose beyond consensus (Kupzog et al., 2020) (Xiong et al., 2023) (Gomez et al., 2019).

**Low Computational Requirements** are fundamental for enabling participation of resource-constrained devices. Effective mechanisms should eliminate the need for specialized hardware and high computational power, instead relying on stake-based validation, voting systems, or authority-based approaches (Meisami et al., 2023) (Caceres et al., 2023) (Cholevas et al., 2024). This ensures that IoT devices and mobile systems can meaningfully participate in consensus without being excluded by hardware limitations (Deep et al., 2024).

**Enhanced Performance Metrics** represent another critical characteristic. Energy-efficient mechanisms should provide improved transaction throughput, reduced latency, and faster confirmation times compared to PoW (Deep et al., 2024) (Zhang et al., 2020) (Xiang et al., 2021). This is particularly important for real-time IoT applications where quick response times are essential (Deepak et al., 2024).

**Scalability Support** should be built into the mechanism design. Effective solutions must handle increasing network sizes and transaction volumes without proportional increases in energy consumption (Abdul, 2024). Techniques like sharding can partition networks into multiple segments to avoid computational overhead duplication across all nodes (Deepak et al., 2024) (Yu et al., 2020).

**Maintained Security** remains non-negotiable despite efficiency gains. Alternative mechanisms must provide robust protection against attacks while avoiding the security vulnerabilities that can emerge from reduced computational barriers (Etemadi et al., 2021) (Xie et al., 2019).
